established_findings.statement: Large language models (LLMs) are actively being researched and applied to NetOps tasks including intent-driven configuration translation, fault diagnosis/AIOps, intent assurance, and multi-agent network management frameworks.
limitations: Most reports are surveys, case studies, or system descriptions rather than wide-scale controlled deployments
Domain specialization (telecom, datacenter, IoT) affects generality

established_findings.statement: Hallucination, factual errors, and unreliable outputs from LLMs are a central reliability concern for operational NetOps use-cases, and active detection/mitigation research exists.
limitations: Detection/mitigation techniques are diverse and evaluated under differing conditions
Few studies report end-to-end operational outcomes for NetOps-specific workflows

established_findings.statement: Tool-augmented and agentic LLM architectures (LLMs invoking verifiers, simulators, or domain tools) are proposed and empirically evaluated as a strategy to improve reliability and functionality for operational tasks.
established_findings.evidence_type: system papers, methodological proposals, and evaluations
limitations: Evaluations vary in scale and task realism
Effectiveness depends on tool quality and integration design

established_findings.statement: Deterministic/formal network configuration verification tools and scalable verifiers (e.g., Batfish-based distributed verifiers) exist and can validate network properties at large scale.
limitations: Verifier applicability depends on the modeled properties (reachability, control-plane simulation) and required abstractions
Distributed verification incurs nontrivial resource/time costs for very large networks

established_findings.statement: Prompt injection and adversarial prompting are recognized threats to LLM pipelines, and practical detection/mitigation frameworks have been proposed and evaluated.
limitations: Defenses are evaluated on specific attack corpora; transfer to NetOps artifacts requires validation
Operational integration and latency trade-offs are not uniformly reported

established_findings.statement: Methodological work highlights the need for standardized evaluation practices for RAG/tool-augmented LLM systems and NetOps-specific benchmarks; several papers propose evaluation blueprints or domain-specific benchmarks (e.g., TelecomGPT).
limitations: Proposed benchmarks are early and domain-specific; no universally accepted NetOps benchmark yet
Blueprints vary in scope and metrics

unresolved_questions.statement: To what degree can LLM-generated network configurations or NetOps actions be executed autonomously in production without unacceptable operational risk?
limitations: One production report (Confucius) describes onboarded apps but does not constitute broad multi-vendor production validation
Surveys flag risks but do not provide quantitative deployment-failure rates

unresolved_questions.statement: Can LLMs reliably self-correct NetOps-specific errors without external deterministic verification signals?
limitations: Evidence suggests self-correction rarely succeeds absent reliable external feedback; NetOps-specific experiments remain limited
Task-dependent: some tasks with external oracles fare better

unresolved_questions.statement: What standardized datasets and metrics best represent operational correctness (safety, policy compliance, reachability) for evaluating LLM-driven NetOps pipelines?
limitations: Multiple proposals exist but consensus and large-scale public corpora for configs are not established in the supplied records
Different operational properties require distinct metrics and validators

candidate_gaps.statement: Systematic empirical evaluations comparing end-to-end generate–validate–repair pipelines (LLM generation + formal verifier + repair loop) against human or traditional automation baselines for NetOps tasks are limited.
limitations: Some frameworks integrate validation (e.g., Confucius) but comparative, reproducible trials at scale are not reported in the supplied records
Variation in task definitions complicates direct comparison

candidate_gaps.statement: Empirically validated adversarial-robustness evaluations and defenses tailored to NetOps artifacts (configs, CLI sequences, topology descriptions) are sparse.
limitations: Existing defenses are evaluated on general prompt-injection corpora; direct tests against NetOps-formatted adversarial inputs are not prominent in supplied records
Operational constraints (latency, tool-call budgets) affect practicability

candidate_gaps.statement: Large, public, realistic corpora of router/device configurations and annotated operational failures for training/evaluating LLMs in NetOps are insufficiently standardized and available.
limitations: Some datasets/topologies are used in verifier papers, but a widely adopted public NetOps-config benchmark is not documented in the supplied records
Data sensitivity and anonymization barriers limit public release

candidate_gaps.statement: Operational cost/latency and tool-orchestration trade-offs (e.g., invoking heavy verifiers or multiple tools per change) require quantification in agentic NetOps pipelines.
candidate_gaps.evidence_type: tool-augmented agent/system papers and queueing/control study for tool-rich agents
limitations: Some analysis exists for tool-rich agents in other domains (queueing/control), but NetOps-specific latency/cost studies are limited in the supplied records
Benefits depend on verifier/tool performance and deployment constraints

excluded_claims: LLMs are proven ready for fully autonomous, unsupervised production NetOps changes without human oversight (no supplied record provides broad, multi-vendor production validation).

There exists a universally accepted, large-scale public benchmark of realistic router/device configurations and annotated operational failures for LLM evaluation (supplied records indicate benchmarking work but not a universally accepted public dataset).

LLMs reliably self-correct arbitrary NetOps mistakes without external deterministic verification signals (evidence suggests self-correction succeeds mainly when reliable external feedback/oracles exist).

Defenses against prompt injection are universally effective across all NetOps-formatted adversarial inputs (supplied defensive studies report strong reductions on their test corpora but not universal effectiveness on NetOps-specific adversarial inputs).
